headline: Heard a presentation from the New Hampshire Municipal Association on conflicts of interest and ethics for local officials.
summary: Attorney C. Christine Johnston of the New Hampshire Municipal Association led the session. It covered incompatibility, conflicts of interest, and public comment rules.
plain_text:
A Special Meeting of the Board of Aldermen was held Monday, November 9, 2026, at 7:00 pm in the Aldermanic 
Chamber and duly noticed in two places, including the City’s website, in accordance with the requirements of RSA 91 -
A:2 II. 
   
President Lori Wilshire presided; Alderman-at-Large Michael B. O’Brien, Sr., recorded. 
 
Prayer was offered by Alderman-at-Large Michael B. O’Brien, Sr.; Alderman Michael B. O’Brien, Sr., led in the Pledge 
to the Flag. 
 
Let’s start the meeting by taking a roll call attendance.   
 
The roll call was taken with 13 members of the Board of Aldermen present:  Alderman Klee, Alderwoman Smith, 
Alderman Thibeault, Alderman O’Brien, Alderman Gregg, Alderman Dowd, Alderman Sullivan, Alderman Sennott, 
Alderman Johnson, Alderwoman Kelly, Alderman Morgan, Alderman Lopez, Alderman Wilshire.    
 
Alderman Clemons and Alderman Ravan were recorded absent. 
 
Corporation Counsel Steve Bolton was also in attendance. 
 
DISCUSSION AND/OR PRESENTATION 
• Conflicts of Interest and Ethics for Local Officials 
President Wilshire recognized Attorney C. Christine Johnston from New Hampshire Municipal Association. 
 
ADJOURNMENT 
 
MOTION BY ALDERWOMAN KELLY THAT THE NOVEMBER 9, 2026 SPECIAL MEETING OF THE BOARD OF 
ALDERMEN BE ADJOURNED 
MOTION CARRIED 
 
The meeting was declared adjourned at 8:41 p.m.             
 
                Alderman-at-Large Michael B. O’Brien, Sr.
P r e s e n t e d  b y :
C .  C h r i s t i n e  J o h n s t o n ,
L e g a l  S e r v i c e s  C o u n s e l
Conflicts of Interest 
and Ethics in Municipal 
Government
N o v e m b e r  9 ,  2 0 2 6
The information presented in NHMA's training 
events and materials is accurate as of the date 
of the presentation. NHMA's training events do 
not constitute legal advice.
For legal advice, city and town officials may 
contact Legal Services at 
legalinquiries@nhmunicipal.org or their own 
municipality's legal counsel. Please refer to 
NHMA's Legal Services FAQ for details about 
how our service works.
For Government Finance Advice, please contact 
financeinquiries@nhmunicipal.org.
Introductory Thoughts
• Municipal government can be challenging!
• The public doesn’t always understand what you 
do, what you’re allowed to do, what you can’t do
• They have no idea how hard it is
• Officials have different priorities or ideas about 
how to accomplish things
• The law is complicated and changes frequently
• And yet – judges expect you to be reasonable and 
follow the law, even when no one else does.
Introductory Thoughts
• At the same time, local officials have to be 
concerned not only about following the law, but 
also about how things look.
• Once the public has lost trust in local officials, it can 
be very difficult to regain it.
• Just because something is legal doesn’t mean it is a 
good idea. Spend a few moments thinking about 
how things appear to the public.
What We’ll Look at Today:
General “Ethics” Issues
Incompatibility
Conflicts of Interest
First Amendment & Civility Issues
Ethical Issues
What Are “Ethics?”
“Ethics” means different things to different people:
• Avoiding conflicts of interest
• Disclosing financial interests
• Avoiding criminal behavior, following the law
• Respecting confidentiality
• Not abusing authority
• Treating people fairly and equally
• Honesty, integrity, and trustworthiness
• Avoiding the appearance of impropriety
Ethics in Public Service
• Public interest, not private gain
• Objectivity and fairness
• Honesty
• Respect for municipal assets and 
taxpayer funds
• Upholding the public trust
• Code of ethics
What Is the Law?
• Incompatibility statutes contain clear rules, but 
they are not the only ethical rules.
• Case law provides a number of examples not 
contained in statute, but even that isn’t complete.
• Ethical Guidepost:
• If you were to read about the same scenario 
occurring somewhere else in the news, would 
you feel good about everyone who participated?
• If the answer is “no,” then take steps to fix it.
Criminal Statutes
• RSA Ch. 640 (Corrupt Practices) prohibits all state and local officials 
and employees from offering, accepting, or failing to report 
bribery, and from engaging in improper influence (threatening 
harm to a person to influence someone’s actions). Class B felonies.
• RSA Ch. 643 (Abuse of Office) (both misdemeanors):
• Official Oppression: knowingly committing an unauthorized act 
or failing to carry out a duty, while purporting to be acting 
officially, to benefit oneself or others.
• Misuse of Information: speculation, acquisition, or sale of 
property with inside knowledge obtained by virtue of public 
office (government “inside trading”).
• RSA Ch. 641 (Tampering with Public Records) prohibits knowingly 
making false entry or alteration of a public record. Class A 
misdemeanor.
Oath of Office
• Oath in Part I, Art. 84 of NH Constitution
• Required for municipal officials (RSA 42:1)
• Bear true faith and allegiance to US and NH
• Uphold the constitutions of both
• Faithfully and impartially discharge and perform 
all duties according to laws and constitution of 
New Hampshire.
• RSA 42:1-a – superior court petition for removal 
from office for violation of oath of office
Oath of Office
• RSA 42:1-a: it is a violation of the oath of office, 
punishable by removal from office, for a local official 
to disclose to the public any information learned by 
virtue of their official position or in the course of 
official duties, if:
• That information is in properly sealed nonpublic 
meeting minutes; or
• The official knew or reasonably should have 
known that the information was exempt from 
disclosure under RSA 91-A:5 and that disclosure 
would satisfy the test for sealing minutes.
Privacy and Governmental 
Records
• RSA 91-A: purpose is public access to information 
about what the government is up to.
• Governmental records contain personal 
information that does not tell the public anything 
about what the government is doing.
• RSA 91-A:5, IV: private v. public balancing test to 
determine whether disclosure of personal 
information would constitute an invasion of privacy
• Some information may need to be redacted
Discussing Official Matters
• RSA 91-A:2-a:
• Public bodies must deliberate about official matters 
in properly-held meetings.
• Communications between meetings “shall not be 
used to circumvent the spirit and purpose” of RSA 
91-A.
• Purpose: “to ensure the greatest possible public 
access to the actions, discussions, and records of all 
public bodies, and their accountability to the 
people.” RSA 91-A:1.
Business Transactions
• RSA 95:1 : Public Officials Barred from Certain Private 
Dealings – No person holding a public office, as 
such, in state or any political subdivision 
governmental service shall, by contract or 
otherwise, except by open competitive bidding, buy 
real state, sell or buy goods, commodities, or other 
personal property of a value in excess of $200 at 
any one sale to or from the state or political 
subdivision under which he holds his public office.
Acting as a Board
• Municipal boards (of all kinds) act officially only as a 
board. Individual members can be authorized by the 
board to take certain actions, but otherwise no single 
member has authority to act
• RSA 49-C:19 – governing body shall act in all matters as a 
body and shall not interfere with duties of other officials
• RSA 46:7 – Mayor and aldermen shall compose one 
board, and shall sit and act together as one body
• Charter: § 47-a, Board of Aldermen shall act in all matters 
as a body; no interference or individual influence with 
mayor or other officers; no direct orders or interference 
with administrative service departments
Incompatibility and 
Conflicts of Interest
Incompatibility
• Refers to whether a person can hold two positions 
at the same time
• RSA 669:7 – general town statute
• RSA 673:7 – planning boards
• Charter § 58:
• No Alderman shall be eligible to hold any other 
municipal office except acting Mayor or 
volunteer firefighter
• No board or commission shall select one of its 
members for any paid position (except as 
otherwise authorized)
Incompatibility
• Common Law: positions may be incompatible even 
if no law or charter or ordinance calls for it
• Whenever two positions bear a special relationship 
to each other, one being subordinate to and 
interfering with the other, with inconsistent 
loyalties or responsibilities, then one person cannot 
legally hold both positions.
• Cotton v. Phillips, 56 N.H. 220 (1875).
• Examples: one position supervising the other (being 
their own boss), one position judging the actions of 
the other (Building Inspector on ZBA)
Conflicts of Interest
• Even where there is no statute or local provision, a 
disqualifying conflict of interest may exist.
• A direct personal or financial interest in the 
outcome of a matter
• May arise from another position they hold, a 
relationship, a bias, another matter in which 
they participated, etc.
• The interest is immediate, definite, and capable of 
demonstration; not remote, uncertain, contingent, 
or speculative. Atherton v. Concord, 109 N.H. 164 
(1968)
Conflicts of Interest
• A situation in which the personal/financial interest 
is or may be in conflict with the public interest
• “A person cannot serve 2 masters at the same 
time.”
• There is nothing illegal or improper about having a 
conflict of interest, so long as it is handled correctly.
• The person with the disqualifying conflict should 
recuse themselves, not abstain.
• However, it is generally up to the person with the 
conflict to recuse themselves.
Conflicts of Interest
• Land Use Boards:  RSA 673:14, prohibits any 
member of a planning board, ZBA, building code 
board of appeals, heritage, historic district, 
agricultural, or housing commission from 
participating in any “judicial” matter if they have a 
direct personal or pecuniary interest in that matter, 
or if they would be disqualified for any reason to sit 
as a juror on the case if it were in court.
• RSA 673:3 and 673:7 require PB/ZBA member to 
recuse themselves from a matter before one board 
if they voted on that case on the other board.
Local Conflict Provisions
• RSA 49-C:33: City charters may include provisions 
relating to conflicts of interest so long as any 
provisions adopted are at least as stringent as the 
state general laws relative to conflicts of interest.
• RSA 31:39-a: Towns (and cities) may adopt conflict of 
interest ordinances which regulate conflicts of 
interest for officials and employees
• Financial disclosures, more stringent 
incompatibility standards, conditions which 
warrant removal from office by court
What if the Person 
Participates Anyway?
• A court may invalidate the actions of a board if a 
person with a disqualifying conflict participated.
• This may depend on whether it was a legislative 
action or a judicial action
• Possible criminal consequences, or if land use 
board, attorneys’ fees and administrative costs
• Disregarding conflict of interest could be seen as an 
ethical violation and a violation of an elected or 
appointed official’s oath of office
Legislative vs. Quasi-Judicial Decisions
Legislative Quasi-Judicial
 Widely felt
 Policy decisions
 Must act in public’s 
interest, but don’t 
need to be 
“indifferent”
 Affect rights of 
specific petitioner
 Notify & hear 
parties
 Weigh evidence
 Must be 
indifferent
What if the Person 
Participates Anyway?
• Courts resolve conflict of interest disputes by 
examining the facts of the conflict (was the person 
really disqualified?) and the type of action involved.
• Legislative decisions (broad issues of public policy) 
– court will only invalidate the action if the person 
with the conflict cast the deciding vote
• Judicial decisions – court will automatically 
invalidate the action and remand to do again 
without the disqualified person
Recusal v. Abstaining
• Recuse: person immediately removes themselves 
from participating with the board on the matter in 
their capacity as a member. Participates, if at all, 
only as a member of the public (or a party).
• Abstaining: person is participating as a member of 
the board in the discussion and hearing (if any) but 
does not vote.
• When there is a conflict, recusal is the remedy. 
Abstaining from the vote is not enough!
Avoiding Conflicts
• Not all conflicts are avoidable, but some issues can 
be minimized.
• Judicial matters – behave as a judge would. Do not 
express opinions publicly or on social media.
• If unsure, disclose the potential conflict early. If no 
one objects, they will likely have waived their right 
to raise a conflict of interest challenge later.
• Ask board for a non-binding vote on recusal.
• When in doubt, consider stepping down.
• Recuse rather than abstaining.
1st Amendment and 
Civility Issues
Free Speech Issues
• 1st Amendment to US Constitution: 
“Congress shall make no law…abridging the freedom 
of speech….”
• Part I, Article 22 of NH Constitution:
“Free speech and liberty of the press are essential to 
the security of freedom in a state; they ought, 
therefore, to be inviolably preserved.”
Free Speech
• Free speech rights may be triggered in a variety of 
settings:
▪ Public Meetings
▪ Public Buildings and Property
▪ Media (official “media” and social media)
• It isn't unlimited, but it does go pretty far.
• Government officials and employees are required to 
deal with unpleasant speech.
Meeting v. Hearing
Meeting
• To conduct the 
board’s business
• RSA 91-A applies
• Open to public
• No right to speak
Hearing
• To hear public or certain 
people on an issue
• Occurs within a public 
meeting
• RSA 91-A “plus”
• Some right to speak
• Right to speak
Who Can Speak?
• Public Meeting: no one other than board members has the 
right to speak, unless the board gives them that right.
• RSA 91-A:2 only grants the right to attend and record.
• Remember – the purpose of a public meeting is for the 
board to conduct its business, which may or may not 
include hearing from the public. It does not have to!
• Public Hearing: who may speak depends on the hearing.
• Check the statute that applies
• In most cases, it will be the “public” generally
• Both: people CAN record audio and video, without telling you.
Public Comment
• Establish written rules as a board (boards may differ).
• Explain the rules clearly at every meeting in which 
comment will be permitted. Repeat as necessary. 
Have written copies.
• Apply the rules evenly to everyone and consistently at 
each meeting (every time).
• The rules can be changed (for future meetings) if they 
aren’t working.
• Try to allow it at consistent times in the agenda 
rather than moving it all around.
1st Amendment Issues
• Once a board allows public comment, First Amendment 
rights have been triggered
• Boards MAY impose “reasonable time, place and 
manner” restrictions on public comment that are 
unrelated to the speech’s content so long as restrictions 
are narrowly tailored to serve a compelling government 
interest and leave open ample alternative channels of 
communication.
• Content-based restrictions may be permissible when 
they preserve the purposes of the limited public forum, 
but viewpoint discrimination is not permitted.
What Restrictions Are Allowed?
• Specific topics (the proposal to make a particular 
street one-way; anything on the agenda; 
anything within the jurisdiction of this board)
• This creates a “limited public forum” for speech
• Time limits per person (3-5 minutes is common 
and generally upheld)
• Using signup sheet or lining up at microphone
• Everyone speaks once before anyone goes again
• No repetitive comments
What Is Not Acceptable?
• “No negative comments”
• No “offensive” comments
• No swearing or obscenity (although specific threats of 
harm may be prohibited)
• Prohibiting a particular person or group from 
speaking (discrimination)
• Prohibiting the display of a message (shirt with 
slogan, banner held up in the back, etc.) without 
disruptive conduct
Can Anyone Speak?
• Public meeting is open to the “public” which 
includes everyone.
• Limiting public comment to “residents only” or 
“taxpayers only” may invite needless litigation.
• A board can simply listen and give each 
comment the weight the members believe that 
comment is due.
• Comments from non-residents, or from people 
who won’t give name or address, may carry less 
weight.
Maintaining Control
• If comments are limited to a particular topic and 
speaker goes off-topic, chair reminds them 
(gently but firmly) of the limitation.
• Encourage people to submit comments in 
writing (note that the board will read them all).
• Board members can simply listen. There is no 
obligation to engage in discussion or answer 
questions.
• Remain calm. Take a deep breath. Practice your 
“neutral face” in the mirror.
Maintaining Control
• If a speaker is breaking the rules, chair should remind 
them of the rule and allow them to try again.
• Provide 2-3 chances.
• Take a 5-10 minute recess from the meeting to let 
everyone calm down. You can do this at ANY TIME.
• Board can vote to adjourn the meeting or continue it 
to another time, date place.
• In extreme cases, someone who is preventing the 
business of the meeting from continuing may be 
removed by law enforcement. Use this sparingly!
• State v. Dominic, 117 N.H. 573 (1977).
Civility – A Difficult Issue
• Civil discourse – the free and respectful exchange of 
different ideas, including questioning and disputing, but 
doing so in a way that respects and affirms all speakers, 
even while critiquing their arguments
• Obviously, civil discourse is encouraged.
• However, civil speech can be disruptive (and ultimately 
out of order), while uncivil speech can be protected.
• First Amendment safeguards the right to present 
viewpoints – even when that speech offends and is 
distasteful to others, because “giving offense is a 
viewpoint.” Matal v. Tam, 582 U.S. 218 (2017).
Civility – A Difficult Issue
• Where does each official have a measure of control? 
THEMSELVES.
• Civil behavior and speech are critically important to a 
healthy, functional, and respectful society, and it starts with 
local officials.
• Each one has chosen to be in a position of leadership.
• Those in a position of power who have been given the 
public trust can set an example for others to follow.
• When public officials behave poorly, it has a trickle -down 
effect on the rest of the community. It erodes trust and 
respect.
Setting the Example
• Treat one another courteously
• Listen to one another
• No side conversations, don’t pass notes, avoid texting (it 
may look like a 91-A issue)
• Avoid becoming defensive. “I don’t know but I’ll find out” is 
a perfectly acceptable statement.
• Some disagreement is actually GOOD. Look at all sides – 
that’s the process, so long as it doesn’t get personal.
• Think about how it looks and assume you are being 
recorded at all times.
9 Pillars of Civility*
➢ Be considerate of others’ opinions; it is okay to disagree.
➢ Manage your emotions. Get curious instead of angry.
➢ Silence is not always weakness.
➢ Be kind.
➢ Actively listen.
➢ Consider the impact of your actions, not just the intent.
➢ Ask questions to learn; answer questions with respect.
➢ QTIP – quit taking it personally.
➢ Have empathy.
*Georgia Municipal Association
